title: APT17
summary: APT17, also tracked as Deputy Dog, is an espionage cluster that public reporting associates with China-nexus operators, with victims mainly in government and defence. Reporting describes strategic web compromise rather than mass phishing: the operators compromise legitimate sites their targets already visit, then use those trusted domains to host command-and-control instructions disguised as ordinary web content. Infrastructure has been reused across campaigns separated by years, which is why analysts group the activity instead of treating each incident as unrelated. Attribution rests on shared infrastructure and timing rather than conclusive evidence, and public reporting presents it as a judgement held with moderate confidence. A trusted domain is not a trusted file, so destination reputation will not help.

beginner.definition: APT17 is a research name for a cyber spying group that public reports link to China. It is also called Deputy Dog. It hides its control messages inside ordinary websites, including sites it runs itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most network tools block connections to known bad servers. This group avoids that by using normal websites that people already visit. Traffic to those sites looks harmless, so alerts stay quiet. It also breaks into websites to reach visitors, which harms the site owner too. This means you need to watch behaviour on the endpoint, not only the addresses your network talks to.
howItWorks: The attackers find websites that their chosen targets already visit often and trust.
They break into those sites, or they build their own sites that look similar.
They place hidden instructions inside ordinary page content that nobody ever questions.
A program on the victim machine opens those pages just like a normal browser.
It finds the instructions, follows them, and sends results back the same way.
Because the site is real and popular, the traffic raises no alarm.
beginner.example: Imagine a message drop hidden in the classified adverts of an ordinary newspaper. A field agent buys the paper each morning, reads a normal-looking advert, and understands the instruction inside it. Anyone watching the newsagent sees only a person buying a newspaper, which is completely ordinary. No secret meeting, no strange location, and nothing unusual to report. Hiding control messages in real websites is the same trick. The channel is public and unremarkable, so the exchange passes unnoticed among all the other traffic.
takeaways: Attackers can hide instructions inside normal websites.
Blocking bad addresses does not help when the address is legitimate.
Watch process behaviour, not only the destinations it contacts.

objectives: Explain how hiding command-and-control in legitimate web content evades destination-based blocking.
Describe why a compromised popular website gives an operator reach beyond a single target.
Identify endpoint and content inspection approaches suited to this technique.
Explain how shared infrastructure supports attribution in public reporting and where it is weak.
Describe the impact on the compromised website owner.
Explain why network reputation services give limited value against this activity.
